title: Sort a Chain by Merging
statement:
You get the head of a singly linked list of integers. Return the head of the same values sorted in ascending order. Equal values stay; nothing is dropped.

The target is O(n log n) time. Lists are shown as arrays, so [3, 1, 2] means 3 → 1 → 2. An empty list is [].

examples.why: Both 3s are kept, and the negative value moves to the front.
An empty list is already sorted; return null.
Reverse order is the worst case for insertion into a list: every new node walks the whole sorted part. Merge sort does not care.

hints: Which O(n log n) sort does not need random access by index? Quick sort and heap sort jump around; one classic sort only ever walks forward.
Merge sort: split the list in half, sort each half, merge. Find the middle with a slow and a fast pointer and cut the link there.
Merging two sorted lists needs no extra nodes: a dummy head and a tail pointer that you keep attaching the smaller front node to.

explain.intuition:
Linked lists have no index access, which hurts quick sort and heap sort, but merge sort only walks forward. And merging is easier on lists than on arrays: you re-point next links instead of copying values into a buffer.

Split the list at its middle (slow pointer one step, fast pointer two steps; when fast hits the end, slow is at the middle), cut the link, sort both halves recursively, and merge them. Each level of recursion does O(n) work and there are log n levels.
steps: If the list has zero or one node, return it.
Find the node before the middle with slow and fast pointers (start fast one step ahead so a two-node list splits in two).
Merge them behind a dummy node and return dummy.next.
pitfalls: Starting fast and slow at the same node. On a two-node list slow stays on the second node, the left half never shrinks and the recursion never ends.
Forgetting to cut the link between the halves, so the left half still runs into the right half.
Not attaching the leftover part of one list after the merge loop.

solutions.title: Insertion into a sorted chain
solutions.idea: Take nodes one by one and splice each into place in a growing sorted list. Simple, but every insert may walk the whole sorted part.

solutions.title: Top-down merge sort
solutions.idea: Split at the middle with slow and fast pointers, sort each half recursively, merge by relinking nodes.

followups: Do it with O(1) extra memory: merge bottom-up, first runs of length 1, then 2, 4 and so on, with no recursion.
Why is merge sort the natural choice for linked lists while quick sort is often faster for arrays?
